analysis.one_liner: Lets borrowers refinance high-interest private student loans into lower-rate federal loans.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a temporary program letting certain borrowers swap private student loans for federal Direct Consolidation Loans. Eligible borrowers — mostly people enrolled between 1994 and 2010 who took at least one private loan while also eligible for federal unsubsidized Stafford or PLUS loans — could pay off their private loan balances with a federal loan at a lower, weighted-average federal interest rate, gaining federal repayment protections. The government would pay private lenders in full for the balances refinanced. The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee in July 2011, sent to a subcommittee in September, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers carrying private student loan debt from 1994-2010 who are current on their loans (or in a grace period, or who defaulted during 2007-2009 due to economic hardship). They would trade private loans — which typically carry higher, variable rates and fewer protections — for a federal Direct Consolidation Loan at a lower weighted-average rate, with federal loan terms and protections. The Department of Education would run outreach so eligible families know the program exists.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers with private student loan debt

how_it_helps.text: Eligible borrowers could consolidate eligible private education loans — disbursed between July 1, 1994 and July 1, 2010 — into a Federal Direct Consolidation Loan, exchanging private loan terms for federal ones.

The new federal loan would bear interest at a weighted-average federal rate (based on Direct Unsubsidized Stafford or Direct PLUS rates in effect the day before enactment), rounded up to the nearest one-eighth of one percent — generally well below the variable rates many private loans carried.
Borrowers who defaulted on federal or private loans during the 2007-2009 recession due to economic hardship would still be eligible, targeting relief at people hit hardest by the downturn.
The bill requires the Education Department to actively publicize the program through a website, alumni outreach, and help for colleges, using plain and language-appropriate materials.
The Secretary of Education would pay each private loan holder the full consolidated amount, and the holder would discharge that portion of the borrower's debt.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through an open-ended appropriation ('such sums as may be necessary') to pay private lenders the full balance of every refinanced loan and to absorb the risk on the resulting federal loans. Private lenders would also lose the future interest income from loans paid off early, though they are made whole on principal. Borrowers not meeting the narrow eligibility rules get nothing.

drawbacks.text: The authorization is open-ended — 'such sums as may be necessary' are appropriated — so the program's cost to taxpayers depends entirely on how many borrowers participate, with no cap in the bill.

Eligibility is narrow: borrowers in default are generally excluded (with a hardship exception only for defaults between December 2007 and December 2009), loans disbursed after July 1, 2010 do not qualify, borrowers must have a clean credit record for PLUS purposes, and the amount consolidatable is capped by formulas tied to federal loan limits.
The program is temporary — it would begin 30 days after enactment and expire on June 30, 2012, leaving only months to run outreach and process applications.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers who qualify, the swap is genuinely valuable: a lower fixed-weighted federal rate and federal protections instead of private loan terms. The honest costs are that taxpayers bear an uncapped outlay paying private lenders in full and taking on the resulting federal loans, that many of the most distressed borrowers (those in default outside the 2007-2009 hardship window) are excluded, and that the program's six-month-to-one-year window is very short for a nationwide refinancing effort.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and then to its higher education subcommittee, and no committee vote, floor vote, or further action ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edolphus Towns introduced the College Debt Swap Act of 2011 on July 6, 2011, joined by eight cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day, and on September 8, 2011 was referred to the Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training.
No further action was recorded: the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and died at the end of the 112th Congress in January 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders keep collecting interest on private loans that would have been refinanced at federal rates, and taxpayers avoided the uncapped cost — but eligible borrowers got no relief.

for.name: Edolphus Towns
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

against.name: John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee the bill was referred to never held a markup or vote on it; it sat in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all nine cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-controlled Education and Workforce Committee; no vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Private student loan lenders (banks and finance companies)
industries.note: The bill would pay these lenders the full outstanding balance of refinanced loans, but they would lose the high-interest private loans that are among their more profitable products. Their interest in keeping private loans outstanding runs against borrowers seeking cheaper federal terms.

industries.industry: Federal Direct Loan program (Department of Education)
industries.note: The program would route refinanced private debt through federal Direct Consolidation Loans, expanding the federal loan book. Borrowers would gain federal protections, while taxpayers take on the credit risk.
